note: 201/9-01's sprite change, flown on the device against its own control — and the answer is that it buys nothing this device can resolve. Filed because a null result costs the same to take as a positive one and is worth more than the change it refuses to justify.
device: MGA-LX3 / ARM Bifrost @ DPR 2, css 360x320, ?surface=720x640 pinned on every window
pose: [1500,-1500] h900 pitch -1.15 yaw pi perspective — ONE settled pose, held identical across all six windows. Not the ten-leg route: this arm is about a CPU span that the camera path does not change, and holding the pose still removes a variable the route would add.

arms.board: the shipping path since 2026-09-05 — each mark rasterized once into a sprite and blitted per instance
arms.nosprites: `?sprites=0`, the layer's own fallback — the mark rebuilt as a path per instance, which is what shipped before. Proven NON-NULL in every window by `symbology.spriteVariants` reading 0 against the sprite arm's 6-9.

reading.verdict: INDISTINGUISHABLE. board 7.014 / 6.162 / 5.971 (range 1.04 ms), nosprites 6.429 / 6.103 / 6.542 (range 0.44). The sprite arm's own spread SPANS the control arm's entirely, and the sign of the difference flips with the pairing: windows 1-2 read -0.58 ms in the control's favour, windows 5 and 6 read +0.57 in the sprite arm's.
reading.whatTheSequenceActuallyShows: the first four windows fall monotonically — 7.014, 6.429, 6.162, 6.103 — while the arm alternates. That descent is warm-up and caching, not the lever, and reading windows 1-2 alone would have filed a confident -0.58 ms result. Third time this repository has had three windows agree on a false story.
reading.whyItWasPredictable: the desk control (2026-09-05-desk-canvas-symbol-arms) put the whole effect at 0.03-0.06 ms per 150 marks. This session's spread on the same span is ~1 ms. The lever was always going to be an order of magnitude under the floor, and the desk number said so before the device did.
reading.modelsAreNotAConfoundHere: `drawUnit` draws its chevron whether or not a 3D model exists under it, so `overlay:symbols` is the same work at unitsAsModels 0 and 150. Windows 4-6 are the ones taken with the fleet loaded throughout and they carry the same verdict as the whole set.

theFindingThatMatters.claim: the drawing is a MINORITY of this span, so neither arm was ever going to move it.
theFindingThatMatters.evidence: 150 marks cost ~0.3 ms of canvas work at a desk. Even at a large device penalty that is one or two of these six milliseconds. The rest is what the layer does per unit AROUND the drawing: two projections and their allocations, `gtaToEngine` twice, `aheadOf`, a colour string built per unit per frame, a sprite cache key built per unit per frame, a hit-area object, a rank object — 190 times a frame, at ~50 fps.
theFindingThatMatters.next: split `symbology.render` the way `overlay-2d` was split, and attribute the 6 ms before optimising any part of it. Making the overlay's own split permanent this session is what turned this line from an unattributed remainder into a number at all.

owed: the decision on whether the sprite path stays the default. It is not a regression and it is provably less work per instance; it is also a module, a cache, a fallback and an arm that this device cannot show a reason for.
